title: A live payment key committed to the repository
summary: A routine dependency audit flagged a credential pattern in the checkout service.

brief.subject: Secret scanner hit on checkout-service, needs a human
brief.body:
Hi,

Our secret scanner flagged something in checkout-service overnight. It is a high-confidence match on a payment provider key pattern, but the scanner cannot tell live keys from sandbox ones, so I need someone who knows the code to look.

Worth knowing before you start: this repository is public. It was open-sourced eight months ago as part of the developer relations push, and the commit history went public with it.

If it turns out to be a live key, do not just delete the line and push. Come and find me first, because deleting it does not do what people think it does.

Daniel
objectives: Determine whether a real credential is exposed and where it came from
Work out the true blast radius, including the repository's history
Choose a response that actually revokes the attacker's access

debrief.rootCause: A live payment provider secret key was hardcoded into config/index.ts as a temporary workaround when the sandbox environment was unavailable, and the TODO to move it into an environment variable was never actioned. The .env.example file shows the intended pattern, which makes the hardcoded value an exception somebody made under time pressure rather than a misunderstanding.
debrief.businessImpact: The key authorises refunds against the live payment account, so anyone holding it can move real money out of the business. The repository is public, so the key must be treated as compromised by an unknown number of parties from the moment it was pushed. Because git stores every commit, the secret remains readable in the history even after the line is deleted, and public repositories are continuously scraped by automated credential harvesters, typically within minutes of a push.
debrief.remediation: Rotate the key at the provider first: revocation is the only action that actually removes the attacker's access, and every other step is cosmetic until it is done. Then move the new key into an environment variable, review the provider's audit log for unauthorised refunds since the commit landed, and add secret scanning to CI so the next one is caught before it merges rather than eight months after.

files.code:
# Copy to .env and fill in.
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
SESSION_SECRET=change-me
PORT=3000

# Payments
# PAYLANE_SECRET_KEY=

options.text: config/index.ts line 20 — a live secret key assigned as a string literal
payments.client.ts line 14 — the Authorization header sends a bearer token
config/index.ts line 4 — DATABASE_URL is read without a default

questions.explanation: Line 20 assigns a literal beginning pl_live_, and the comment above it says plainly that it is the live key. The .env.example entry is empty and is exactly what should have been used. The Authorization header is correct code doing its job with a value it should never have been given.
hints: Three of these files read configuration. Only one of them contains a value.
Compare how the payment key is supplied against how DATABASE_URL is supplied.
Look for a string literal whose prefix tells you which environment it belongs to.

questions.prompt: The repository is public. Why is deleting the line in a new commit not enough?

options.text: Git keeps every earlier commit, so the key stays readable in the history and in any existing clone or fork
The deployed containers cache the old config until they are rebuilt
The key is also compiled into the frontend bundle and served to browsers
GitHub takes up to 24 hours to purge deleted lines from its search index

questions.explanation: A deletion is just another commit; the blob containing the secret is still in the history and in every clone and fork already out there. This is why the only meaningful first step is rotating the key at the provider. Rewriting history helps with tidiness but cannot un-publish something that has already been fetched.
hints: What does a git commit do to the previous state of the file?
Think about who already has a copy, and whether your commit reaches them.

questions.prompt: What is the correct first action?

options.text: Delete the line, move the key to an environment variable, and open a PR
Rotate the key at the payment provider immediately, then move the new key to an environment variable
Force-push a rewritten history that removes the commit, then rotate the key next sprint
Make the repository private and keep the key where it is until the next release

questions.explanation: Rotation is the only step that removes the attacker's access; everything else is housekeeping that leaves a working key in the wild. Rewriting history first spends hours while the live key stays valid, and making the repository private does nothing about the copies already taken.
hints: Rank the options by one question: which one stops a key that is already stolen from working?
Assume the key was harvested minutes after the push. Which action still helps?

ethicalChoices.text: Rotate the key, then tell the payments team and your manager that a live credential was public for eight months and the provider's audit log needs reviewing.
ethicalChoices.outcome: The conversation was uncomfortable and took most of an afternoon. The audit showed no unauthorised refunds, which meant the disclosure was a near miss rather than an incident. Finance had it in writing that the exposure was found and closed by the team, and secret scanning went into CI the following week.

ethicalChoices.text: Rotate the key quietly and push the environment variable change without mentioning how long it was exposed.
ethicalChoices.outcome: The immediate risk was closed, which mattered. But four months later a routine audit found the original commit, and the questions were no longer about the key. Nobody could establish whether the exposure had been reviewed, so the provider was notified late and the finance team had to assume the worst about eight months of refunds. The engineer who quietly fixed it was the one asked to explain the silence.

ethicalChoices.text: Follow Daniel's instruction to the letter: stop, escalate to him, and take no action on the key until he responds.
ethicalChoices.outcome: Daniel replied within the hour and the key was rotated the same morning, so the delay cost nothing. He noted afterwards that his 'come find me first' was about not deleting the line, not about waiting to revoke — with a live credential public, rotating first and telling him second would also have been right.
